routes.description: Establish that resurrection belief can be reasonable without compelling every observer by applying proportionate standards for unusual historical claims to the reported appearances and their consequences.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the claim contradicts no established fact about Jesus, has the evidence reasonably expected from the alleged event, and is not explained equally well by ordinary alternatives.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative historical case makes belief that Jesus rose from the dead epistemically reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Reasonableness is distinct from personal conviction and should be judged by an objective, proportionate standard.
Early proclamation, communities, writings, and outside notice match the evidence expected if the reported appearances occurred.
Legend, fraud, and mistaken-experience accounts do not explain the principal historical claims as easily as resurrection does.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Paul's early writings and contact with disciples materially constrain a late-legend explanation.
Outsiders, groups, Jewish expectations, and embodied appearance reports make a simple hallucination account less adequate.

routes.description: Establish that accepting an ancient resurrection report is unreasonable because its extraordinary factual content lacks sufficiently testable, independent, and physically corroborated evidence.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the surviving testimonial record is too unverifiable and vulnerable to ordinary human error to justify belief in a bodily resurrection under proportionate evidential standards.

motionBridge.description: The available evidence is insufficient to make belief in Jesus's bodily resurrection reasonable.

centralBridges.description: A reasonable claim must fit established reality and receive evidential support proportionate to its unusual content.
Ancient testimonial reports without physical corroboration or accessible witnesses cannot discharge the resurrection claim's evidential burden.
Deception, mistake, memory failure, and narrative development remain more securely grounded than a supernatural bodily return.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The temporal distance and lack of falsifiable access materially weaken confidence in the reported event.
Additional sincere testimony does not by itself establish that witnesses correctly interpreted what they experienced.

sections.title: Reasonableness, conviction, and standards
sections.rationale: The parties directly contest whether reasonableness is an objective threshold below personal conviction or instead requires consistency with established reality and bias-reducing inquiry.

proMoves.speaker: Trent Horn
proMoves.proposition: Reasonableness differs from being personally convinced, so both sides must offer an objective standard for assessing unusual and unrepeatable events.

sourceSpan.excerpt: I'm going to defend the statement that it's reasonable to believe Jesus of Nazareth rose from the dead. Matt has the burden of defending the negative, that it's not reasonable to believe Jesus rose from the dead. In order for each of us to defend our positions, we each have to present a standard for what makes a belief reasonable, especially belief in unusual, unre repeatable events. However, being reasonable is not the same as being convincing.

proMoves.attributionBasis: This span falls within Horn's uninterrupted opening statement immediately after the moderator explicitly gives him the affirmative floor.

response.rationale: This is Horn's initial framing of the governing epistemic standard and has no earlier selected argumentative target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move expressly distinguishes reasonableness from conviction and confines its demand to unusual, unrepeatable-event beliefs.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The distinction is clear, but the claim that both parties must provide an objective standard is asserted more strongly than the supporting example establishes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between conviction and reasonableness is coherent, though the move compresses the bridge from that distinction to an objective-standard requirement.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The illustrative disagreement supports the conceptual distinction, but it supplies limited warrant for the stronger procedural burden assigned to both debaters.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it directly defines the issue and the evidential task the affirmative proposes to undertake.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially establishes the pro route's central standard bridge rather than yet proving the complete resurrection conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not yet substantively reconstruct or attack a developed live alternative from Dillahunty.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: The opening explicitly states the motion, separates reasonableness from persuasion, and demands a standard suited to unusual historical events.

conMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
conMoves.proposition: Reasonable belief is distinct from truth but should be constrained by what is known possible in reality and by methods that reduce individual bias.

sourceSpan.excerpt: So what's reasonable to believe and what's true are separate, but we're stuck because we may not actually ever have access to the truth. So all we can hope for is what's reasonable. So how do you tell what's reasonable? Well, there's many answers to that and they are all problematic because at the in the end of the day, uh each individual is going to be responsible for determining what's reasonable to them and the rest of society is going to say, Ah, you're unreasonable or you're incredibly reasonable. And so we try to work together. This is one of the reasons why we have scientific methods that remove as much of the bias and subjectivity as possible.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The span is part of Dillahunty's uninterrupted opening statement after the moderator identifies him and starts his allotted time.

components.text: Reasonableness must be distinguished from whether a belief personally convinces someone.
An objective standard should specifically govern unusual and unrepeatable historical-event beliefs.

response.rationale: Dillahunty accepts the truth-reasonableness distinction and supplies a bias-reducing reality constraint, but does not yet answer Horn's specific proposed tests for unusual events.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reality-and-method standard is recoverable, though the relation between individual responsibility and society-wide scientific methods remains somewhat compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Dillahunty acknowledges imperfect access to truth and incomplete removal of subjectivity while advancing a bounded methodological standard.

charity.alternative: Horn distinguishes reasonable belief from personally compelling belief and asks for an objective standard suitable for unusual claims.
charity.decisiveQualification: Horn's opening does not claim that internal consistency or personal conviction alone makes a resurrection belief reasonable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently joins fallible access to truth with collaborative, bias-reducing methods, though individual and social standards are not fully integrated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Scientific bias reduction is an appropriate methodological warrant, but no specific evidence yet shows how that method adjudicates this historical claim.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive distinction and offers a competing standard, while leaving Horn's unusual-event framework substantially unanswered in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the con route's central standard for proportionate and reality-constrained belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves Horn's distinction between truth and reasonableness but does not engage the strongest details of Horn's three-test proposal.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty explicitly concedes that truth and reasonable belief can diverge, then grounds reasonableness in known possibility and bias-reducing methods.

sections.title: Expected evidence and testability
sections.rationale: A central exchange concerns whether the surviving early Christian footprint is exactly what the alleged event predicts or is too inaccessible and unfalsifiable to justify belief.

proMoves.speaker: Trent Horn
proMoves.proposition: If Jesus appeared to the reported witnesses, oral proclamation, churches, some Christian writing, and non-Christian notice without acceptance are the evidence one would expect, and that pattern occurred.

sourceSpan.excerpt: But suppose Jesus really did rise from the dead and appeared to Peter, the 12 disciples, James, Paul, 500 others as recorded in 1 Corinthians 15. What kind of evidence would we expect to emerge after these events? The people to whom Jesus appeared would tell other people about what happened? Some people would believe these disciples and some wouldn't. This process of oral communication would result in the establishment of communities of believers or churches. The tiny minority of believers who were literate might write about the resurrection and non-Christian historians who were aware of this group might reference their beliefs but not accept them.

proMoves.attributionBasis: This is an uninterrupted portion of Horn's timed opening, with stable first-person framing and no intervening speaker transition.

response.rationale: This is Horn's initial constructive argument from the expected historical footprint and therefore has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional claim, predicted forms of evidence, and limited conclusion about reasonableness are all expressly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Horn expressly denies that the pattern proves resurrection, but the fit between a broad social footprint and this particular cause is not uniquely established.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The prediction-to-observation structure is intelligible and qualified, with a remaining bridge from generic movement growth to the specific appearance reports.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited Pauline report and observable rise of communities are relevant, but independence, dating, and rival-cause comparisons remain compressed.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive directly answers the anticipated missing-evidence objection by identifying the historical traces the hypothesis predicts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly advances the pro route's central expected-evidence bridge, while stopping short of the complete motion-level conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing alternative is represented or attacked within this opening constructive span.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Horn specifies several expected consequences of reported appearances and carefully limits the conclusion to absence of a defeating evidential gap.

conMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
conMoves.proposition: A religiously consequential resurrection claim supported only by temporally remote anecdotal material is too unverifiable and unfalsifiable to be reasonably believed.

sourceSpan.excerpt: One might wonder, as I do, if this event actually happened and there's a good and wise God behind it, why did he leave us with such a positive anecdotal evidence and place this event in a such a temporal situation as to make it unverifiable and unfalsifiable? Because I'd argue that an untestable claim of a matter of fact such as this event occurred, no matter what the event is, can never be reasonably believed unless that matter of fact is wholly mundane and when the risk of being wrong is minimized.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The excerpt is within Dillahunty's uninterrupted opening and uses his first-person formulation of the negative evidential standard.

components.text: The predicted oral proclamation and community growth supply a historical footprint if appearances occurred.
The observed footprint is not equally expected from ordinary transmission, error, or movement formation.

response.rationale: Dillahunty directly argues that the surviving footprint is anecdotal and inaccessible, but does not compare Horn's predictions with specific rival explanations in this span.

precisionFindings.rationale: The testability objection is clear, but the categorical phrase concerning any untestable nonmundane fact broadens beyond the historical case argued.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The absolute exclusion of untestable nonmundane claims is stronger than the supplied observations about temporal distance and anecdotal evidence warrant.

charity.alternative: Horn argues that the event predicts oral reports, communities, limited writings, and outside notice rather than modern physical records.
charity.decisiveQualification: Horn expressly presents this expected footprint as defeating an absence objection, not as deductive proof of resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move gives a clear testability principle, but the leap from reduced verification to categorical unreasonableness leaves historical degrees of support underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Temporal distance and inaccessible witnesses support caution, while the universal evidential exclusion is asserted without a defended historical comparison.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive evidential adequacy issue but does not answer whether Horn's specific predicted traces actually occurred or discriminate among causes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the con route's central evidence-insufficiency bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly identifies Horn's reliance on a surviving testimonial footprint, though it compresses his explicitly limited expected-evidence conclusion.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: The move identifies lack of present verification and falsification as reasons the surviving record cannot meet the burden for a consequential extraordinary claim.

sections.title: Historical testimony and movement origins
sections.rationale: The parties contest whether early Pauline contact and rapid community formation materially constrain legend or whether multiplying sincere reports remains epistemically inadequate.

proMoves.speaker: Trent Horn
proMoves.proposition: Late invention is weakened by Paul's writings and contact with disciples, Luke's accounts, and the otherwise unexplained rapid formation of resurrection-centered churches after Jesus's death.

sourceSpan.excerpt: resurrection? The most important evidence would be claims that Jesus appeared in a bodily form to groups of his disciples after death. So, how could we explain these claims? Well, here are four possibilities. One, the claims never happened and were invented by later Christians as a legendary development. The problem with this explanation is that we have Paul's writings and he had contact with the disciples and even makes this claim about himself. We also have accounts from Luke who shows himself to be a very reliable historian and he both documents these appearances and Peter's testimony about the resurrection in Acts 2. Finally, if the disciples never claimed Jesus rose from the dead, then we have no explanation for how church communities based on this belief arose so quickly when other messianic movements fell apart after the death of their leaders.

proMoves.attributionBasis: The span is continuously delivered by Horn during his opening and forms a numbered part of his affirmative alternative analysis.

response.rationale: Horn introduces the early-source and movement-origin case constructively before any selected opposing move addresses it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anti-legend route is recoverable, though 'reliable historian' and the implied dating and independence of the sources are insufficiently specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The sources make early belief plausible, but the claim of no explanation for rapid community formation and the reliability assertion exceed the defended warrants.

charity.alternative: The bodily-appearance claims could have been invented by later Christians through legendary development.
charity.decisiveQualification: A strong legend alternative can allow early experiences or beliefs while disputing later narrative details, not merely deny that disciples made any resurrection claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The early-source inference is intelligible, but it compresses the distinction between early resurrection belief and every later bodily-appearance detail.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Pauline contact and early communities are material evidence, while Luke's reliability, source independence, and the comparative claim about other movements require further defense.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive squarely anticipates and addresses a late-invention alternative with identifiable historical considerations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move supports the necessary subsidiary early-testimony bridge rather than independently completing the affirmative route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The legend alternative is narrowed to claims that never happened, omitting stronger versions that accept early belief while challenging later elaboration.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Horn relies on Paul's contact with disciples, Luke-Acts, and rapid church emergence to argue that resurrection proclamation was not a late invention.

conMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
conMoves.proposition: The number of testimonials is not independently sufficient because sincere people can misinterpret experiences, as illustrated by demon and alien-abduction reports.

sourceSpan.excerpt: plural of anecdote isn't data so it doesn't matter how many testimonials you have that alone is not going to be uh enough and unless you view that in the broader stream of things and the way I've explained this is that like my mom okay screw it I I I don't like doing this but my mom is a fundament fundamentalist Southern Baptist Christian who believes she has seen demons. Okay. Now, I'm happy to believe that my mom thinks that she has seen something, but that doesn't mean that I'm I'm justified in accepting that what she's act that she's correct about what she's seen. Same with people who are abducted by aliens. Um or claim sorry people who claim they're abducted by aliens.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The dialogue immediately identifies Dillahunty's personal example, and Horn's next turn responds to it as Dillahunty's stated epistemology.

components.text: Early and numerous reports can establish sincere belief without establishing the reported event's correct interpretation.
Paul's contact with disciples and rapid church formation specifically constrain a late legendary-development account.

response.rationale: The move directly separates sincerity from truth but does not address the specific dating, contact, or comparative movement-origin evidence Horn adduces.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly limited to testimony alone and clearly distinguishes having an experience from correctly identifying its cause.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move does not deny experiences occurred; it cautiously denies that testimonial quantity alone justifies the witnesses' interpretation.

charity.alternative: Horn's case invokes early Pauline contact, group claims, and rapid movement formation rather than raw testimonial quantity alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: Horn offers historical timing and explanatory context in addition to the number and sincerity of reports.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between sincere experience and accurate causal interpretation is stable and follows directly from the offered comparison.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The demon and abduction examples appropriately demonstrate possible sincere error, but they do not establish close comparability with the early Christian record.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive sincerity-versus-truth component while leaving Horn's specific early-source and movement-origin warrants unanswered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the con route's subsidiary testimonial-quantity bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately addresses testimonial reliance but compresses Horn's broader historical argument into a quantity-of-anecdotes issue.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty concedes sincere experiences while arguing through contemporary analogues that sincerity and testimonial accumulation do not validate interpretation.

sections.title: Mistake, hallucination, and sincerity
sections.rationale: The decisive explanatory comparison concerns whether group, outsider, expectation, and embodiment features defeat ordinary mistake accounts and what persecuted sincerity can actually establish.

proMoves.speaker: Trent Horn
proMoves.proposition: A grief-hallucination account inadequately explains unbelieving outsiders, Jewish resurrection expectations, and reported appearances to groups rather than isolated bereaved individuals.

sourceSpan.excerpt: believe they saw the risen Jesus but they were mistaken. They had some kind of grief induced hallucination. Uh but this explan this doesn't explain any other facts related to Jesus's death. One, we should be skeptical of the disciples being griefstricken. It's equally likely they were angry they wasted years of their life following another failed Messiah. Moreover, Paul and James were not griefstricken over Jesus's death because they weren't believers when he was crucified. Two, since ancient Jews believe the resurrection wouldn't take place until the end of the world, it follows that even if they had griefinduced hallucinations, the disciples would have thought they saw Jesus's soul in heaven, not his glorified body on earth. Moreover, given their fierce monotheism, we would expect them to hallucinate Jesus as a man exalted in heaven and not as the creator himself unless Jesus told them he used divine power to raise himself from the dead. Three, Paul tells us Jesus appeared to groups of people.

proMoves.attributionBasis: Horn delivers this numbered alternative analysis continuously in his opening, with no ambiguity about the affirmative speaker.

response.rationale: This is Horn's initial developed comparison with a mistaken-experience hypothesis and therefore has no prior selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed grief-hallucination model is identifiable, but 'hallucination' covers several possible experiences and some expectations are generalized across disciples.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited differences weaken a simple grief model, but do not by themselves exclude varied experiences, social reinforcement, or later interpretive development.

charity.alternative: Disciples sincerely believed they encountered Jesus but were mistaken through grief-related visionary or hallucinatory experiences.
charity.decisiveQualification: A stronger ordinary account need not posit identical simultaneous hallucinations or require every later narrative detail to originate in one experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative objections form an intelligible comparative case, though several premises move from reported traditions to psychological expectations without fully defended bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul, James, group reports, and Jewish expectations are relevant, but their exact historical form and the psychological generalizations need stronger verification.

responsiveness.rationale: The constructive directly addresses a leading ordinary explanation through several distinct allegedly mismatched features.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It substantially advances the pro route's central alternative-comparison bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move treats the ordinary alternative chiefly as simple grief hallucination and omits stronger mixed models involving interpretation, transmission, and development.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Horn identifies outsiders, prior expectations, and group reports as features he argues a straightforward grief-hallucination hypothesis does not predict well.

conMoves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
conMoves.proposition: Willingness to suffer or die demonstrates strength or presentation of conviction, but has no bearing on whether the underlying resurrection belief is true.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Waco and in uh Ghana and others but the notion that someone is willing to die for something testifies to how strongly they believe how convinced they are or how convinced they want someone to think they are. It has no bearing on whether or not it's actually true.

conMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator's question assigns the response to Dillahunty, and Horn's immediately following answer explicitly agrees with and qualifies Dillahunty's point.

components.text: Paul and James were not bereaved followers and therefore do not fit a simple grief-hallucination model.
Jewish expectations and reported group appearances make the alleged experiences unlike ordinary isolated grief visions.

response.rationale: The move supplies relevant contrary material limiting sincerity evidence, but contacts none of Horn's specific arguments about outsiders, expectations, or group appearances.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move precisely limits the inference from costly commitment to conviction rather than truth and includes the possibility of performed conviction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The core distinction is strong, but saying costly commitment has no bearing at all overstates the point because it can bear indirectly on sincerity-related hypotheses.

charity.alternative: Horn treats persecution as evidence of sincerity that must then be explained, not as direct proof that resurrection occurred.
charity.decisiveQualification: Horn's broader alternative analysis separately invokes outsiders, group reports, expectations, and other historical features.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference-limiting distinction between conviction and truth is clear, although the phrase 'no bearing' overlooks indirect evidential relevance to fraud hypotheses.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Cross-religious willingness to suffer provides appropriate comparative support, but the short span does not document the comparison or its historical similarity in detail.

responsiveness.rationale: It is germane to Horn's ordinary-alternative case but does not contact any indispensable component of the selected hallucination argument.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the con route's central ordinary-error bridge by blocking an inference from sincerity to truth.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately limits what sincerity establishes, though its categorical wording risks implying Horn relied on sincerity as direct proof rather than one explanatory datum.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty uses examples of costly religious commitment to distinguish sincere conviction from the truth of the proposition for which one suffers.
